A repeater extends distance; a hub does not

topics.t: Network topologies
topics.h: If one cable snaps, does your whole office go offline or just one desk? The answer depends on the topology.
p: Topology is the arrangement of nodes and links in a network. Mesh: every node is connected to every other node. n nodes need n(n - 1)/2 links. Very reliable, but costly and hard to cable.
Ring: each node connects to exactly two neighbours, forming a closed loop; data usually travels in one direction. A single break can disrupt the whole ring.
Bus: all nodes share one backbone cable with terminators at the ends. Cheap and needs the least cable, but a fault in the backbone stops the whole network, and faults are hard to find.

Star: every node connects to a central hub or switch. Easy to install, extend and troubleshoot; one node's failure does not affect others, but if the central device fails, the whole network stops. Uses more cable than bus.

Tree (hierarchical): star networks joined by a bus-like backbone, as in a school with a switch on each floor. Choosing a layout in case studies: usually a star from the server building, which keeps cable short and failures contained.

ex.q: How many direct links does a fully connected mesh of 6 computers need?
st: Each of 6 nodes connects to 5 others: 6 × 5 = 30 ends
Each link is counted twice, so divide by 2

topics.rl: An Indian bank's data centres are often linked in a mesh-like way, so that if one link fails, transactions can still flow through another path.

rv.summary: Topology is how nodes are arranged. Mesh connects every node to every other (n(n − 1)/2 links), ring forms a loop, bus shares one backbone, star uses a central device, and tree joins stars in a hierarchy.
focus: Describe mesh, ring, bus, star and tree topologies
Count links in a full mesh
Compare advantages and failure points
Choose a topology for a given layout
remember: Mesh: n(n − 1)/2 links; most reliable, most costly
Ring: closed loop, each node has two neighbours
Bus: one backbone, least cable; backbone fault stops all
Star: central hub/switch; easy to extend; centre fails → all fail; tree = stars joined in a hierarchy
traps: Don't forget to divide by 2 when counting mesh links
In a star, one node's failure does not stop the others
Bus, not star, uses the least cable

topics.t: MAC and IP addresses, the Internet, the Web, IoT and DNS
topics.h: You type ncert.nic.in, but computers only understand numbers like 164.100.x.x. A hidden phone book called DNS makes the switch in milliseconds.
p: MAC address: the unique 48-bit (6-byte) physical address burnt into a NIC, written as 12 hexadecimal digits in six pairs, e.g. 30-9C-23-1B-83-A5. The first half identifies the manufacturer. It does not change when the device moves.

IP address: a logical address given to a device on a network, which can change when it joins another network. IPv4 uses 32 bits written as four numbers from 0 to 255 (192.168.1.10). IPv6 uses 128 bits, written as eight groups of hexadecimal digits, because IPv4 addresses were running out.

The Internet is the global network of networks (the infrastructure). The World Wide Web is one service that runs on it: a collection of linked web pages accessed with browsers. Email and file transfer also use the Internet but are not the Web.
IoT (Internet of Things): everyday objects such as smart meters, ACs, watches and street lights connected to the Internet to send data and be controlled.

A domain name such as www.ncert.nic.in is a readable name for an IP address. The last part is the top-level domain (TLD): generic ones like .com, .org, .edu, .gov, or country codes like .in. DNS (Domain Name System) servers translate domain names into IP addresses; this is called name resolution.

ex.q: Arun types www.isro.gov.in in his browser. Outline what happens before the page loads.
st: The browser asks a DNS server for the IP address of www.isro.gov.in
The DNS server resolves the name and returns the IP address
The browser contacts the web server at that IP address
The server sends the web page back to the browser
ex.a: DNS resolves the name to an IP address, then the browser fetches the page from that server

topics.rl: Smart electricity meters installed by Indian power distribution companies report usage over the network automatically, a real IoT example in many cities.

rv.summary: A MAC address is a fixed 48-bit physical address of a NIC; an IP address is a logical address that can change (IPv4 32 bits, IPv6 128 bits). The Web runs on the Internet, IoT connects everyday objects, and DNS translates domain names into IP addresses.
focus: Tell MAC addresses from IP addresses
Recognise valid IPv4 addresses
Distinguish the Internet from the World Wide Web
Explain DNS and top-level domains
remember: MAC: 48 bits, 12 hex digits, fixed in the NIC
IPv4: 32 bits, four numbers 0–255; IPv6: 128 bits
Internet = network of networks; Web = linked pages on it
DNS resolves domain names to IP addresses; TLD is the last part (.in, .com)
traps: Don't accept an IPv4 part above 255
The Internet and the Web are not the same thing
The TLD of www.cbse.gov.in is .in, not .gov

topics.t: Web services: HTML, XML, URLs, browsers, servers and hosting
topics.h: Every time you open the DigiLocker website, a browser on your phone asks a web server somewhere for an HTML page. Let's open the hood.
p:
WWW: a system of interlinked documents and resources on the Internet. HTML (HyperText Markup Language) uses predefined tags such as

and

to present web pages; it is not case-sensitive.
XML (eXtensible Markup Language) stores and carries data using user-defined tags such as <rollno>; it is case-sensitive and focuses on data rather than display. HTML shows data; XML describes data.

A URL (Uniform Resource Locator) is the address of a resource on the web. In https://www.ncert.nic.in/textbook.php, https is the protocol, www.ncert.nic.in is the domain name and textbook.php is the path to the document.

A web page is a single document on the web; a website is a collection of related web pages under one domain. A web browser (Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Safari) is client software that requests and displays pages; a web server is a computer and software that stores pages and sends them on request.
Web hosting is the service of storing a website's files on a server permanently connected to the Internet, so that anyone can reach the site by its domain name.

ex.q: Identify the parts of the URL https://www.cbse.gov.in/results.html.

topics.rl: An Indian startup launching its website pays a hosting company to keep its pages on servers that run all day and night, so customers from Kashmir to Kanyakumari can open it at any hour.

rv.summary: The WWW is a system of linked documents. HTML presents data with predefined tags, XML stores data with user-defined, case-sensitive tags, a URL gives a resource's address, browsers request pages from web servers, and hosting keeps sites online.
focus: Compare HTML and XML
Identify the parts of a URL
Tell a web page from a website, and a browser from a server
Explain web hosting
remember: HTML: predefined tags, presents data, not case-sensitive
XML: user-defined tags, describes data, case-sensitive ('extensible')
URL parts: protocol (https), domain name, path
Browser requests pages; web server stores and sends them; hosting keeps files on an online server
traps: Don't swap the tag rules of HTML and XML
Don't mix up a website (many pages) with a web page (one)
Apache is web server software, not a browser

topics.t: Case study: designing a network
topics.h: Section E of the board paper almost always describes a company with four buildings and asks you to design its network. There is a reliable method. Here it is.
p: Server location: put the server in the building with the MOST computers. That keeps most traffic inside one building (the 80-20 rule of thumb) and reduces cabling.
Cable layout: usually a star from the server building to every other building, which keeps cable short and failures contained. Write it as a simple diagram.
Repeater: place one on any cable run longer than about 100 m (Ethernet's limit). Hub or switch: one in EVERY building, to connect its computers. A switch is preferred over a hub.

Joining distant sites: within a campus use Ethernet cable or optical fibre; across hilly or distant places (hundreds of km) use satellite, microwave or radio links. Network type: buildings within a campus form a LAN; offices in different cities form a WAN.
Common difference questions: hub vs switch, LAN vs WAN, MAC vs IP, circuit vs packet switching, and matching each device to its function.

ex.q: A school has four blocks with these computer counts: Admin 30, Science 90, Junior 40, Library 15. Distances from Science: Admin 120 m, Junior 80 m, Library 60 m. Where do the server and repeaters go?
st: The Science block has the most computers (90), so the server goes there
Use a star layout from Science to the other three blocks
Only the Science–Admin run (120 m) is longer than 100 m, so place a repeater on it
Put a switch in every block
ex.a: Server in Science; repeater on the Science–Admin link; a switch in each block

topics.rl: Large Indian hospitals such as AIIMS run campus networks linking OPD blocks, labs and wards. Planners follow exactly these rules to decide where the main server and switches go.

rv.summary: In network case studies, place the server in the building with the most computers, use a star layout from it, add repeaters on runs over about 100 m and a switch in every building, and choose media like optical fibre or satellite based on distance.
focus: Choose the server building
Decide where repeaters and switches go
Suggest a cable layout
Choose a transmission medium and network type
remember: Server in the building with the most computers
Star layout from the server building
Repeater on runs longer than about 100 m; switch in every building
Campus → LAN; cities → WAN; far, hilly places → satellite or microwave; high speed, no interference → optical fibre
traps: Don't put the server in the middle building by default
Don't put repeaters on every link
Don't choose Bluetooth or infrared for long distances; they are very short-range

topics.t: Data communication: components, bandwidth and data rate
topics.h: A WhatsApp message from Kolkata reaches Kochi in under a second. Five simple components make that possible, and two numbers measure how fast.
p: Data communication is the exchange of data between two or more devices over a transmission medium.

Its five components: sender (the device that sends), receiver (the device that receives), message (the data: text, audio, video and so on), communication media (the path, wired or wireless) and protocols (the agreed rules both sides follow).
Bandwidth is the range of frequencies a channel can carry, measured in hertz (Hz). 1 KHz = 1000 Hz, 1 MHz = 1000 KHz, 1 GHz = 1000 MHz. Higher bandwidth means more data can be carried.

Data transfer rate (bit rate) is the number of bits sent per second, measured in bps. NCERT uses binary multiples: 1 Kbps = 2^10 bps = 1024 bps, 1 Mbps = 1024 Kbps, 1 Gbps = 1024 Mbps, 1 Tbps = 1024 Gbps.
Remember bytes and bits: 1 byte = 8 bits. File sizes are usually in bytes (MB), while speeds are in bits per second (Mbps).

ex.q: How long does it take to send a 10 MB file over an 8 Mbps link? (Use 1 MB = 1024 × 1024 bytes and 1 Mbps = 1024 × 1024 bps.)

topics.rl: When your broadband plan says '100 Mbps', it is quoting a data transfer rate. A movie file of a few GB still takes minutes, because the file size is in bytes and every byte is 8 bits.

rv.summary: Data communication is the exchange of data between devices over a medium, with five components: sender, receiver, message, communication media and protocols. Bandwidth is a frequency range in hertz, and data rate is bits per second (NCERT: 1 Mbps = 1024 Kbps).
focus: Name the five components of data communication
Explain bandwidth and its units
Convert data-rate units the NCERT way
Find file transfer time from size and rate
remember: Components: sender, receiver, message, communication media, protocols
Bandwidth: Hz; 1 KHz = 1000 Hz, 1 MHz = 1000 KHz
Data rate: bps; 1 Kbps = 1024 bps, 1 Mbps = 1024 Kbps, 1 Gbps = 1024 Mbps
1 byte = 8 bits: time = file size in bits ÷ rate
traps: Bandwidth is in hertz, not bytes or bps
Use 1024 (NCERT), not 1000, for data-rate units
Don't divide bytes by a rate in bps; convert bytes to bits first

topics.t: Simplex, half-duplex, full-duplex and switching
topics.h: A walkie-talkie makes you say 'over' after every sentence. A phone call doesn't. The difference has a name.
p: Simplex: data flows in one direction only. Examples: keyboard to computer, computer to printer or monitor, a radio broadcast.
Half-duplex: both directions, but only one at a time. Example: a walkie-talkie.
Full-duplex: both directions at the same time. Examples: a telephone or mobile call, a video call.
Circuit switching: a dedicated path is set up between sender and receiver before communication begins and is kept for the whole session, as in a traditional landline call.

Packet switching: data is split into small packets that may travel by different routes and are reassembled in order at the destination. No dedicated path is reserved, so the links are shared efficiently. The Internet uses packet switching.

ex.q: Classify: (a) a TV broadcast, (b) a police walkie-talkie, (c) a video call on your phone.
st: (a) data flows only from the station to your TV → simplex
(b) both can talk, but one at a time → half-duplex
(c) both talk and hear at once → full-duplex

topics.rl: When you watch a cricket match stream on your phone, the video arrives as thousands of packets that may take different routes across India's networks and are reassembled in your app.

rv.summary: Simplex sends data one way only, half-duplex both ways but one at a time, and full-duplex both ways at once. Circuit switching reserves a dedicated path; packet switching sends packets by different routes over shared links, as on the Internet.
focus: Classify devices as simplex, half-duplex or full-duplex
Explain circuit switching
Explain packet switching
Compare their use of network links
remember: Simplex: keyboard, printer, TV/radio broadcast
Half-duplex: walkie-talkie; full-duplex: phone or video call
Circuit switching: dedicated path for the whole session (landline)
Packet switching: packets may take different routes, reassembled at the destination (Internet)
traps: Phone calls are full-duplex, not half-duplex
Packets may arrive out of order; no fixed path is reserved
The Internet uses packet switching, not circuit switching

topics.t: Guided media: twisted pair, coaxial and optical fibre
topics.h: The cable behind your router, the one into your set-top box, and the fibre that BharatNet laid to villages: three wired media, three different strengths.
p: Transmission media are of two kinds: guided (wired), where signals travel along a physical cable, and unguided (wireless), where signals travel through air or space as electromagnetic waves.

Twisted pair cable: pairs of insulated copper wires twisted together to reduce interference. UTP (unshielded) is cheap and used in LANs and telephone lines; STP (shielded) has extra shielding for less noise. It is cheap, flexible and easy to install, but has lower bandwidth and its signal weakens over long distances.

Coaxial cable: a central copper conductor, an insulating layer, a braided metal shield and an outer jacket. Better shielding and higher bandwidth than twisted pair; used for cable TV. It is costlier and less flexible than twisted pair.

Optical fibre: carries data as pulses of light through a thin glass or plastic core, kept inside by total internal reflection. Very high bandwidth, very low loss over long distances, immune to electromagnetic interference and hard to tap, but costly and delicate to install and repair.
Choosing: twisted pair for cheap short LAN links; coaxial for cable TV; optical fibre for long, high-speed backbones and noisy places.

ex.q: Which wired medium would you choose between two data centres 5 km apart that need very high speed and no interference from nearby power lines?
st: Twisted pair weakens over long runs and picks up noise
Coaxial is better shielded but still electrical
Optical fibre carries light: very high bandwidth and immune to electromagnetic interference

topics.rl: BharatNet, India's project to bring broadband to gram panchayats, lays optical fibre because it carries huge amounts of data over long distances with little loss.

rv.summary: Guided media are cables: twisted pair (cheap, for LANs), coaxial (better shielded, for cable TV) and optical fibre (light pulses, very high bandwidth, no interference, but costly). Unguided media travel through air.
focus: Tell guided from unguided media
Describe twisted pair, UTP/STP and coaxial cable
Describe optical fibre and its pros and cons
Choose a medium for a situation
remember: Twisted pair: twisted to reduce interference; UTP cheap, STP shielded
Coaxial: copper core, insulation, braided shield, jacket; cable TV
Optical fibre: light by total internal reflection; high bandwidth, low loss, no EMI
Fibre is costly and delicate to install
traps: Optical fibre is wired (guided), not wireless
Fibre is the most expensive wired medium, not the cheapest
Don't choose copper cable where there is heavy electrical noise; choose fibre

topics.t: Wireless media: radio waves, microwaves, infrared, Bluetooth and WLAN
topics.h: Your TV remote fails if someone stands in front of it, but your FM radio works in the kitchen. They both use waves; the difference is which waves.
p: Radio waves: omnidirectional (spread in all directions), travel long distances and can pass through walls. Used in AM/FM radio, cordless phones and wireless networks.

Microwaves: unidirectional and need line of sight between sending and receiving antennas, which are mounted high on towers. They cannot pass through solid obstacles well. Used for satellite links, mobile phone networks and long-distance point-to-point links.
Infrared waves: very short range and line of sight; they cannot pass through walls. Used in TV remote controls and some short-range device links. A plus: the signal stays inside the room.
Bluetooth: short-range (about 10 m) wireless technology using radio waves, for PANs such as phone to earbuds, keyboards and smartwatches.
Wireless LAN (Wi-Fi): computers connect without cables through an access point, which is linked to the wired network or the Internet.

ex.q: Which wireless medium suits each: (a) a TV remote, (b) a satellite link for a DTH service, (c) an FM radio station?
st: (a) very short range, line of sight, stays in the room → infrared
(b) line of sight, high frequency, dish to satellite → microwave
(c) spreads in all directions and through walls → radio waves

topics.rl: DTH television dishes on Indian rooftops point at a satellite in the sky: that line-of-sight microwave link is why heavy monsoon rain can briefly interrupt the signal.

rv.summary: Wireless media: radio waves spread in all directions and pass through walls, microwaves need line of sight from tall towers, infrared is short-range and blocked by walls, Bluetooth links devices within about 10 m, and Wi-Fi connects through an access point.
focus: Compare radio waves, microwaves and infrared
Give uses of each wireless medium
Know Bluetooth's range and use
Explain why microwave towers are tall
remember: Radio: omnidirectional, through walls (FM, cordless phones)
Microwave: line of sight, tall towers (satellite, mobile networks)
Infrared: very short range, cannot pass walls (TV remote)
Bluetooth: about 10 m (PAN); Wi-Fi: wireless LAN via an access point
traps: Microwaves are not omnidirectional
TV remotes use infrared, not radio
Bluetooth is short-range, not kilometres

topics.t: Mobile generations and protocols: HTTP, HTTPS, FTP and PPP
topics.h: India's first mobile phone call was made in 1995, and 5G was launched here on 1 October 2022. Along the way, a handful of protocols kept every device speaking the same language.
p: 1G (1980s): analog, voice calls only. 2G: digital voice with SMS and MMS (GSM, CDMA). 3G: mobile Internet, video calls and faster data. 4G: high-speed mobile broadband for HD streaming and online gaming. 5G: very high speed, very low latency, and connections for huge numbers of devices (IoT).

A protocol is a set of rules for communication: it fixes the format of messages, their timing and sequence, and how errors are checked. Without common protocols, devices from different makers could not understand each other.

HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol) transfers web pages between a browser (client) and a web server through requests and responses. HTTPS is the secure version: data is encrypted, shown by the padlock in the address bar. Use it for banking and payments.
FTP (File Transfer Protocol) transfers files between computers, for example uploading website files to a hosting server.
PPP (Point-to-Point Protocol) runs on a direct link between two nodes, such as a dial-up or leased line connecting a computer or router to an ISP.

ex.q: Which protocol fits each task: (a) opening a news website, (b) paying a bill on a bank website, (c) uploading 50 files to a web server?

topics.rl: Government sites such as the income-tax e-filing portal use HTTPS, so your PAN and bank details are encrypted on the way to the server.

rv.summary: Mobile generations grew from analog voice (1G) to digital SMS (2G), mobile Internet (3G), broadband (4G) and low-latency IoT (5G). Protocols are communication rules: HTTP and HTTPS for web pages, FTP for files and PPP for direct links.
focus: Match features with mobile generations
Explain why protocols are needed
Choose between HTTP and HTTPS
Know the uses of FTP and PPP
remember: 1G analog voice; 2G digital, SMS/MMS; 3G mobile Internet; 4G broadband; 5G very low latency, IoT
Protocol: rules for format, timing, sequence and error checking
HTTP transfers web pages; HTTPS encrypts them (padlock)
FTP transfers files; PPP works on a direct link between two nodes
traps: SMS came with 2G, not 1G
Plain HTTP is not secure for payments
PPP is not a web or email protocol

topics.t: Protocols: SMTP, POP3, TCP/IP, TELNET and VoIP
topics.h: Sending an email and reading one use two different protocols. Mixing them up is one of the most common one-mark slips in the board paper.
p: SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) SENDS email: from your mail program to the mail server, and between mail servers.
POP3 (Post Office Protocol version 3) RECEIVES email: it downloads messages from the mail server to your device.

TCP/IP: TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) breaks a message into packets, numbers them, checks for errors and reassembles them reliably at the destination, asking for lost ones again. IP (Internet Protocol) gives each packet the address information needed to route it to the right device.

TELNET lets a user log in to a remote computer and work on it through text commands (remote login). VoIP (Voice over Internet Protocol) carries voice calls as data packets over the Internet, as in WhatsApp or Google Meet calls.
Exam-style tasks: identify the communication mode, choose a transmission medium for a case, pick the protocol for a task, and convert data-rate units.

ex.q: Meera sends an email from Gmail to Arjun, who downloads it into his mail app. Which protocols are involved?
st: Meera's message travels to her mail server and on to Arjun's server using SMTP
Arjun's app downloads it from his mail server using POP3
Underneath, TCP/IP splits, routes and reassembles the packets
ex.a: SMTP to send, POP3 to receive, over TCP/IP

topics.rl: Every WhatsApp voice call you make to a cousin abroad is VoIP: your voice is turned into data packets and carried over the Internet instead of the old telephone network.

rv.summary: SMTP sends email and POP3 receives it. TCP splits data into packets and reassembles them reliably, while IP addresses and routes them. TELNET gives remote login and VoIP carries voice calls over the Internet.
focus: Tell SMTP from POP3
Explain the jobs of TCP and IP
Know TELNET and VoIP
Match tasks with protocols and convert data rates
remember: SMTP: send email; POP3: receive (download) email
TCP: packets, ordering, error checking, resending lost packets
IP: addressing and routing
TELNET: remote login; VoIP: voice over the Internet
traps: Don't swap SMTP and POP3
Reliability comes from TCP, not IP; IP does not encrypt
Voice calls use VoIP, not TELNET

topics.t: Why databases? Limits of the file system
topics.h: A school keeps student details in one file, fees in another and attendance in a third. Then a student changes her phone number, and only one file gets updated. Chaos begins.
p: Organisations such as schools, banks and hospitals must store and manage large amounts of data (student attendance, accounts, patients) in an organised way, so it can be found and updated quickly.
In a file system, data is kept in separate files, each created and handled by its own program. This leads to problems.

Difficulty in access: there is no easy way to ask a new question of the data; a new program must be written each time. Data redundancy: the same data (a student's name and address) is stored in several files, wasting space.

Data inconsistency: redundant copies stop matching when one is updated and another is not. Data isolation: related data is scattered over files of different formats, so combining it is hard. Data dependence: the programs depend on the file's exact structure, so changing the format means rewriting the programs.
Controlled data sharing is difficult: it is hard to give each kind of user (clerk, teacher, principal) access to only the data they should see.

ex.q: A student's address is stored in both the fee file and the library file. The fee office updates it; the library does not. Name the two problems shown.
st: Storing the address in two files is data redundancy
The two copies now disagree, which is data inconsistency

topics.rl: Imagine railway booking clerks in different cities each keeping a separate register for the same train: the same berth could easily be sold twice. A single shared database prevents that.

rv.summary: Organisations must store large amounts of data in an organised way. File systems keep data in separate files, causing difficulty in access, data redundancy, inconsistency, isolation, dependence and poorly controlled sharing.
focus: Name the limitations of the file system
Identify each limitation from an example
Explain how redundancy leads to inconsistency
Contrast file systems with DBMS benefits
remember: Redundancy: same data stored in several files
Inconsistency: copies of the same data disagree
Isolation: data scattered in different files and formats; dependence: programs tied to the file structure
Difficult access: a new program for each new question; controlled sharing is hard
traps: Don't swap cause and effect: redundancy is the cause, inconsistency the effect
Isolation does not mean the data is secret
Easy SQL querying is a DBMS advantage, not a file-system limitation

topics.t: Database Management System and its key terms
topics.h: When you check your board result online, a DBMS finds your one record among lakhs in a fraction of a second.
p: A database is an organised collection of related data. A DBMS (Database Management System) is software used to create, store, manage and retrieve data in databases. Examples: MySQL, Oracle, PostgreSQL, SQL Server, Microsoft Access.
Applications: banking (accounts, transactions), railway and airline reservation, library management, school records, hospital patient records, online shopping inventories.

Database schema: the design or structure of the database (names of tables, their attributes, data types, constraints and relationships). Data constraint: a rule restricting the values that can be stored, such as NOT NULL or UNIQUE. Meta-data (stored in the data dictionary or catalog): data about the data, for example the schema itself.
Database instance: the actual data in the database at a particular moment. The schema changes rarely; the instance changes with every insert, update or delete.

Query: a request to retrieve or change data (written in SQL). Data manipulation: inserting, updating and deleting data. Database engine: the core software component that stores the data, runs queries and enforces constraints.

ex.q: A school database has a table STUDENT(RollNo, Name, Class). On Monday it holds 400 rows; on Friday, 405. What is the schema, and what changed?
st: The schema is the structure STUDENT(RollNo, Name, Class) with its data types and constraints
The schema stayed the same during the week
The instance (the data present at a moment) changed from 400 to 405 rows
ex.a: Schema: the table's structure; the instance changed

topics.rl: IRCTC's ticketing runs on a DBMS that handles a huge number of bookings at once and stops two passengers from being given the same berth.

rv.summary: A database is an organised collection of related data and a DBMS is software to create, store, manage and retrieve it, like MySQL. Key terms: schema (structure), instance (data at a moment), constraint, meta-data, query, data manipulation and database engine.
focus: Define a database and a DBMS with examples
Tell schema from instance
Know constraints and meta-data
Know queries, data manipulation and the database engine
remember: DBMS examples: MySQL, Oracle, PostgreSQL, SQL Server, MS Access
Schema = design or structure; instance = data at a particular moment
Constraint = rule on values (NOT NULL, UNIQUE); meta-data = data about data (data dictionary)
Data manipulation = insert, update, delete
traps: Inserting a row changes the instance, not the schema
A DBMS is software, not hardware
A fact like '50 rows' is not a constraint

topics.t: The relational data model: relations, tuples, degree and cardinality
topics.h: Every SQL question starts with a table. Learn to read a table the way the relational model does, and degree and cardinality become free marks.
p: In the relational model, data is stored in relations (tables) made of rows and columns.
Attribute: a column (e.g. Name). Tuple: a row (one record). Domain: the set of allowed values for an attribute (e.g. Class from 1 to 12).
Degree: the number of attributes (columns). Cardinality: the number of tuples (rows). A table with 5 columns and 30 rows has degree 5 and cardinality 30.

Properties of a relation: every attribute has a unique name; the order of attributes does not matter; every tuple is distinct (no two rows are identical); the order of tuples does not matter; each value is atomic (a single value, not a list) and comes from the attribute's domain.
NULL is a special value meaning 'unknown' or 'not applicable'. It is not zero and not an empty string.

ex.q: A table CUSTOMER has the columns CustID, Name, City, Phone and holds 120 customers. Find its degree and cardinality.

topics.rl: An Aadhaar-style registry can be imagined as one giant relation: each person is a tuple and attributes such as name and date of birth are columns.

rv.summary: In the relational model, data is stored in relations (tables): attributes are columns, tuples are rows and a domain is the set of allowed values. Degree is the number of columns and cardinality the number of rows; values are atomic and NULL means unknown.
focus: Identify attributes, tuples and domains
Find degree and cardinality
Know the properties of a relation
Use NULL correctly
remember: Attribute = column; tuple = row; domain = allowed values
Degree = number of columns; cardinality = number of rows
Tuples are distinct; order of rows and columns does not matter; values are atomic
NULL = unknown or not applicable (not 0 or '')
traps: Don't swap degree and cardinality
Rows need not be sorted
A list cannot be stored in one cell

topics.t: Keys: candidate, primary, alternate, composite and foreign
topics.h: Two students named Priya Sharma in the same class? The database doesn't panic, because it never relies on names. It relies on keys.
p: Candidate key: an attribute (or set of attributes) whose values uniquely identify each tuple, e.g. RollNo, AadhaarNo or Email in a STUDENT table.
Primary key: the candidate key chosen to identify tuples. It must be unique and cannot be NULL. Alternate keys: the candidate keys that were not chosen as the primary key.

Composite primary key: a primary key made of two or more attributes, used when no single attribute is unique. In ATTENDANCE(RollNo, AttDate, Status), neither RollNo nor AttDate alone is unique, but (RollNo, AttDate) is.

Foreign key: an attribute in one relation that refers to the primary key of another relation, linking the two. Referential integrity: every foreign-key value must match an existing primary-key value in the referenced table (or be NULL, where allowed).
Exam tasks: identify the candidate, primary, alternate and foreign keys and the degree and cardinality of given tables, and list the differences between a file system and a DBMS.

ex.q: Tables: STUDENT(RollNo, Name, Email, ClassID) and CLASS(ClassID, ClassTeacher). Roll numbers and emails are both unique. Identify the keys.
st: Candidate keys of STUDENT: RollNo and Email
Choose RollNo as the primary key, so Email is an alternate key
ClassID is the primary key of CLASS
ClassID in STUDENT refers to CLASS, so it is a foreign key
ex.a: Primary key RollNo, alternate key Email, foreign key ClassID

topics.rl: A bank uses your account number as a primary key. Your transactions table stores that account number as a foreign key, so every transaction links back to exactly one account.

rv.summary: A candidate key uniquely identifies each tuple; the chosen one is the primary key (unique, not NULL) and the rest are alternate keys. A composite key uses several attributes, and a foreign key refers to another table's primary key under referential integrity.
focus: Identify candidate, primary and alternate keys
Choose a composite primary key
Identify foreign keys between tables
Explain referential integrity
remember: Primary key: chosen candidate key; unique and not NULL
Alternate keys = candidate keys not chosen
Composite key: two or more attributes, e.g. (RollNo, AttDate)
Foreign key refers to another table's primary key; it may repeat
traps: A unique non-primary attribute is an alternate key, not a foreign key
A foreign key need not be unique in its own table
Don't count the primary key as an alternate key

topics.t: SQL basics, command categories, data types and constraints
topics.h: SQL is the one language that banks, railways, hospitals and your school's result system all speak. You tell it WHAT you want; it works out HOW.
p: An RDBMS (relational DBMS) stores data in related tables. Popular ones: MySQL, Oracle, Microsoft SQL Server, PostgreSQL. CBSE uses MySQL.
SQL (Structured Query Language) is declarative: you state what data you want, not the steps to get it. Keywords are case-insensitive (SELECT = select), and each statement ends with a semicolon.
DDL (Data Definition Language) defines or changes structure: CREATE, ALTER, DROP. DML (Data Manipulation Language) works on the data: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE; SELECT queries the data.

Data types: CHAR(n) is fixed length: it always uses n characters, padding shorter values with spaces. VARCHAR(n) is variable length, up to n characters, using only what the value needs. INT for whole numbers, FLOAT for decimals, DATE in 'YYYY-MM-DD' format.

Constraints: NOT NULL (a value is required), UNIQUE (no duplicates), DEFAULT (a value used when none is given), PRIMARY KEY (unique and not NULL; identifies each row), FOREIGN KEY (must match a primary key in another table).

ex.q: Choose data types for Aadhaar number (always 12 digits), name (up to 40 characters, length varies) and date of birth.
st: The Aadhaar number has a fixed length and is not used in arithmetic: CHAR(12)
Date of birth: DATE, entered as 'YYYY-MM-DD'

topics.rl: A bank's accounts table might make the account number the PRIMARY KEY and declare the balance column NOT NULL, so no two accounts share a number and no account is left without a balance.

rv.summary: SQL is a declarative, case-insensitive language for RDBMSs like MySQL. DDL (CREATE, ALTER, DROP) changes structure and DML (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE) changes data. Key types are CHAR, VARCHAR, INT, FLOAT and DATE, and constraints include NOT NULL, UNIQUE, DEFAULT, PRIMARY KEY and FOREIGN KEY.
focus: Classify commands as DDL or DML
Choose between CHAR and VARCHAR
Write DATE values correctly
Know what each constraint does
remember: DDL: CREATE, ALTER, DROP; DML: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE (SELECT queries)
CHAR(n): fixed length, padded; VARCHAR(n): variable, up to n
DATE format: 'YYYY-MM-DD'
PRIMARY KEY = UNIQUE + NOT NULL; DEFAULT supplies a value when none is given
traps: Don't swap the categories: ALTER is DDL; UPDATE is DML
Don't think CHAR(10) stores 'Ram' in 3 characters; it uses all 10
Don't think SQL keywords are case-sensitive; they are case-insensitive

topics.t: Data definition: CREATE, USE, DESCRIBE, ALTER and DROP
topics.h: Before a single record goes in, someone has to build the shelves. DDL is SQL's carpentry.
p: Databases: CREATE DATABASE School; SHOW DATABASES; USE School; (selects it for use) DROP DATABASE School; (deletes it and all its tables).
CREATE TABLE STUDENT (RollNo INT PRIMARY KEY, Name VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL, Class INT, City VARCHAR(20) DEFAULT 'Delhi'); SHOW TABLES; lists the tables in the current database.
DESCRIBE STUDENT; or DESC STUDENT; shows the structure: column names, data types, NULL allowed or not, keys and defaults.
ALTER TABLE changes structure: ADD Phone CHAR(10); DROP Phone; ADD PRIMARY KEY (RollNo); DROP PRIMARY KEY; ADD FOREIGN KEY (ClassID) REFERENCES CLASS(ClassID); MODIFY Name VARCHAR(40);
DROP TABLE STUDENT; removes the table completely: its structure and its data. DELETE FROM STUDENT; (DML) removes only the rows and leaves the empty table.

ex.q: Add a column Email of type VARCHAR(50) to the table STUDENT, then view the new structure.
st: ALTER TABLE STUDENT ADD Email VARCHAR(50);
ex.a: ALTER TABLE STUDENT ADD Email VARCHAR(50); then DESC STUDENT;

topics.rl: When a hospital decides to start recording each patient's ABHA health ID, the database team runs an ALTER TABLE ... ADD statement rather than rebuilding the whole patient table.

rv.summary: DDL commands create and change structure: CREATE DATABASE, USE, SHOW, CREATE TABLE, DESC, ALTER TABLE (ADD, DROP, MODIFY, ADD PRIMARY KEY, ADD FOREIGN KEY) and DROP TABLE. DROP removes a table completely, while DELETE only removes rows.
focus: Create and select databases and tables
View structure with DESC
Change structure with ALTER TABLE
Tell DROP TABLE from DELETE FROM
remember: USE School; selects the database; SHOW TABLES; lists tables
DESC STUDENT; shows the structure
ALTER TABLE ... ADD / DROP / MODIFY column; ADD PRIMARY KEY (col)
FOREIGN KEY (ClassID) REFERENCES CLASS(ClassID)
traps: Use ALTER, not UPDATE, to add a column
Don't use ADD to change an existing column; MODIFY changes it and ADD creates a new one
Don't mix up DROP TABLE (removes structure and data) with DELETE (keeps the table)

topics.t: Data manipulation: INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE
topics.h: Forget the WHERE clause in an UPDATE and every employee in the company gets the same salary. Ask any database admin about their worst day.
p: INSERT INTO STUDENT VALUES (101, 'Asha', 12, 'Pune'); gives values for every column, in the table's column order.
INSERT INTO STUDENT (RollNo, Name) VALUES (102, 'Ravi'); gives values only for the listed columns; the others get NULL or their DEFAULT. Text and dates go in single quotes.
With foreign keys, insert into the referenced (parent) table first. A STUDENT row with ClassID 12 is rejected unless CLASS already has ClassID 12.
UPDATE STUDENT SET City = 'Agra' WHERE RollNo = 101; changes matching rows. Without WHERE, every row is updated. UPDATE changes data (DML); ALTER changes structure (DDL).
DELETE FROM STUDENT WHERE RollNo = 101; removes matching rows. Without WHERE, all rows are deleted, but the empty table remains.

ex.q: Give every employee in the IT department a 10% raise in the table EMP(EmpID, Name, Dept, Salary).
st: Use UPDATE, because it changes existing data
WHERE Dept = 'IT' limits it to IT
ex.a: UPDATE EMP SET Salary = Salary * 1.10 WHERE Dept = 'IT';

topics.rl: When the government revises dearness allowance, payroll teams run a single UPDATE with a WHERE clause instead of editing lakhs of salary records by hand.

rv.summary: INSERT adds rows (with a column list when giving only some values), UPDATE ... SET ... WHERE changes rows and DELETE ... WHERE removes rows. Without WHERE, UPDATE and DELETE affect every row, and parent tables must be filled before child tables.
focus: Write INSERT with and without a column list
Write UPDATE with SET and WHERE
Write DELETE with WHERE
Respect foreign-key order and tell ALTER from UPDATE
remember: INSERT INTO T VALUES (...) needs a value for every column
INSERT INTO T (c1, c2) VALUES (...) fills only listed columns
UPDATE T SET col = value WHERE condition;
DELETE FROM T WHERE condition; (no WHERE → all rows deleted, table stays)
traps: Don't leave out WHERE in UPDATE unless every row must change
Don't insert into the child table before the parent
Don't mix up ALTER (changes structure) with UPDATE (changes data)

topics.t: SELECT: columns, aliases, computed columns and DISTINCT
topics.h: SELECT is the most-used SQL word on the planet. Every app that shows you a list, from Zomato's menus to your exam timetable, runs one.
p: SELECT * FROM EMP; shows all columns. SELECT Name, City FROM EMP; shows only the chosen columns, in the order you list them.
Computed columns: SELECT Name, Salary * 12 FROM EMP; works out a value for each row without changing the stored data.
Column alias with AS: SELECT Name, Salary * 12 AS AnnualSalary FROM EMP; renames the column heading in the output. An alias containing spaces goes in quotes: AS "Annual Salary".
DISTINCT removes duplicate values from the output: SELECT DISTINCT City FROM EMP; lists each city once.
SELECT never changes the table: it only displays a result.

ex.q: From EMP(Name, Dept, Salary, City) with cities Delhi, Pune, Delhi, Mumbai, Pune, Delhi, list each city once.
st: Duplicates must go, so use DISTINCT
Result: Delhi, Pune and Mumbai (3 rows)
ex.a: SELECT DISTINCT City FROM EMP; gives 3 rows

topics.rl: A food-delivery app shows each cuisine once in its filter menu even though thousands of restaurants serve it: that is a DISTINCT query.

rv.summary: SELECT shows chosen columns, computed columns and aliases without changing the table. AS renames output headings (quotes for spaces), and DISTINCT removes duplicate values or combinations.
focus: Select specific columns
Write computed columns with aliases
Use DISTINCT on one or more columns
Predict the number of rows returned
remember: SELECT col1, col2 FROM T; shows chosen columns
SELECT Salary * 12 AS Annual FROM T; computes without changing data
Alias with spaces: AS "Annual Salary"
DISTINCT removes duplicate values (or combinations, for several columns)
traps: A computed column does not change stored data
Don't leave out the quotes around an alias with spaces
DISTINCT on two columns works on the pair, not just the first column

topics.t: WHERE with operators, BETWEEN, IN and NULL
topics.h: WHERE Salary = NULL looks right but returns nothing, every single time. NULL plays by its own rules.
p: WHERE filters rows using relational operators (=, <, >, <=, >=, <> or !=), logical operators (AND, OR, NOT) and arithmetic in conditions (e.g. WHERE Salary * 12 > 600000).
BETWEEN a AND b selects values in a range, including both ends: WHERE Salary BETWEEN 40000 AND 55000 includes 40000 and 55000.
IN checks membership in a list: WHERE City IN ('Delhi', 'Pune'). NOT IN selects values outside the list.
NULL means unknown, so = NULL and <> NULL are never true. Use IS NULL and IS NOT NULL: WHERE Salary IS NULL.
AND is evaluated before OR; use brackets to make your meaning clear.

ex.q: EMP(Name, Dept, Salary, City): Asha HR 40000 Delhi; Ravi IT 55000 Pune; Meena IT 60000 Delhi; Kabir Sales 35000 Mumbai; Zoya HR NULL Pune; Dev IT 50000 Delhi. Which names does SELECT Name FROM EMP WHERE City = 'Delhi' AND Salary > 45000; show?

topics.rl: A bank's fraud desk might query WHERE Amount > 100000 AND City NOT IN ('Mumbai', 'Delhi') to spot unusual high-value transactions.

rv.summary: WHERE filters rows using relational, logical and arithmetic conditions. BETWEEN includes both ends, IN and NOT IN test a list, and NULL must be tested with IS NULL or IS NOT NULL, since = NULL is never true.
focus: Write WHERE conditions with AND, OR and NOT
Use BETWEEN, IN and NOT IN
Test for NULL correctly
Use arithmetic inside conditions
remember: BETWEEN a AND b includes a and b
IN ('Delhi', 'Pune'); NOT IN for values outside the list
Use IS NULL / IS NOT NULL, never = NULL
AND is evaluated before OR
traps: Don't exclude the boundary values; BETWEEN includes them
= NULL returns no rows
NULL values do not satisfy range conditions

topics.t: Pattern matching with LIKE and sorting with ORDER BY
topics.h: Find every customer whose name starts with 'S' and list them from the highest bill down: two tiny clauses, LIKE and ORDER BY, do it.
p: LIKE matches text patterns using two wildcards: % stands for any number of characters (including none), and _ stands for exactly one character.
'A%' starts with A; '%a' ends with a; '%an%' contains 'an'; '_a%' has a as the second letter; '____' (four underscores) is exactly four characters long. NOT LIKE excludes a pattern.
ORDER BY sorts the result: ORDER BY Salary; is ascending (ASC, the default) and ORDER BY Salary DESC; is descending.
Sorting on several columns: ORDER BY Dept, Salary DESC; sorts by Dept first and, within each department, by Salary from high to low.
ORDER BY comes after WHERE in a query: SELECT ... FROM ... WHERE ... ORDER BY ...;

ex.q: From EMP, list the names starting with 'M' or ending with 'a', in alphabetical order. (Names: Asha, Ravi, Meena, Kabir, Zoya, Dev.)
st: WHERE Name LIKE 'M%' OR Name LIKE '%a'
'M%' matches Meena; '%a' matches Asha, Meena and Zoya
ORDER BY Name sorts them alphabetically

topics.rl: When you type 'Pan' in a railway station search box, the app may run something like WHERE StationName LIKE 'Pan%' to suggest Panvel and Panipat.

rv.summary: LIKE matches patterns with % (any number of characters, even none) and _ (exactly one character). ORDER BY sorts results ascending by default or descending with DESC, and can sort on several columns.
focus: Write LIKE patterns for starts, ends, contains and fixed length
Use ORDER BY ASC and DESC
Sort on two columns
Place ORDER BY after WHERE
remember: 'A%' starts with A; '%a' ends with a; '%an%' contains an
'_a%' has a as the second letter; '____' is exactly four characters
ORDER BY col (ascending by default); ORDER BY col DESC
ORDER BY Dept, Salary DESC: DESC applies only to Salary
traps: Don't use = with wildcards; use LIKE
Don't think % needs at least one character; it can match zero characters
Don't think ORDER BY sorts descending by default; the default is ascending

topics.t: Aggregate functions and NULL
topics.h: COUNT(*) and COUNT(Salary) can give different answers on the same table. The difference is one NULL, and it is a favourite board question.
p: Single-row functions work on each row separately and return one value per row (e.g. UPPER(Name)); you only need to know this difference, because single-row functions are not in the CBSE CS exam syllabus. Aggregate (multi-row) functions work on a group of rows and return one value for the whole group.
Aggregates: MAX(col) largest value, MIN(col) smallest, SUM(col) total, AVG(col) average, COUNT(col) number of non-NULL values in the column.
COUNT(*) counts all rows, including rows with NULLs. COUNT(col) skips NULLs. COUNT(DISTINCT col) counts the different non-NULL values.
SUM, AVG, MAX and MIN ignore NULL values. So AVG(col) = SUM(col) / COUNT(col), not divided by COUNT(*).
Aggregates can be combined with WHERE: SELECT AVG(Salary) FROM EMP WHERE Dept = 'IT'; averages only the IT rows.

ex.q: EMP(Name, Dept, Salary): Asha HR 40000; Ravi IT 55000; Meena IT 60000; Kabir Sales 35000; Zoya HR NULL; Dev IT 50000. Find COUNT(*), COUNT(Salary), SUM(Salary) and AVG(Salary).

topics.rl: At the end of an IPL season, the stats team runs MAX(Runs) for the Orange Cap, SUM(Runs) for team totals and AVG for batting averages, all aggregate functions.

rv.summary: Aggregate functions MAX, MIN, SUM, AVG and COUNT return one value for a group of rows. COUNT(*) counts all rows, COUNT(col) skips NULLs, and SUM, AVG, MAX and MIN ignore NULL values.
focus: Compute MAX, MIN, SUM, AVG and COUNT on a table
Tell COUNT(*) from COUNT(col) and COUNT(DISTINCT col)
Handle NULL values in aggregates
Combine aggregates with WHERE
remember: COUNT(*) counts all rows; COUNT(col) counts non-NULL values
AVG(col) = SUM(col) / COUNT(col)
SUM, AVG, MAX and MIN ignore NULL
Single-row functions (UPPER, LENGTH) give one value per row
traps: Don't treat NULL as 0 in averages
COUNT(*) does not skip NULL rows
MIN ignores NULL, so it is not 0

topics.t: GROUP BY and HAVING
topics.h: 'Total sales per region', 'average marks per section', 'number of trains per zone': every 'per' in a question is a hint to use GROUP BY.
p: GROUP BY col puts rows with the same value of col into one group; aggregate functions then give one result per group: SELECT Dept, COUNT(*) FROM EMP GROUP BY Dept;
Columns in the SELECT list should be either the grouping column(s) or aggregates.
HAVING filters groups after grouping, using aggregate conditions: ... GROUP BY Dept HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
WHERE filters individual rows BEFORE grouping and cannot use aggregate functions; HAVING filters groups AFTER grouping.
Clause order: SELECT ... FROM ... WHERE ... GROUP BY ... HAVING ... ORDER BY ...;

ex.q: EMP(Name, Dept, Salary): Asha HR 40000; Ravi IT 55000; Meena IT 60000; Kabir Sales 35000; Zoya HR NULL; Dev IT 50000. Find the number of employees and total salary in each department.
st: SELECT Dept, COUNT(*), SUM(Salary) FROM EMP GROUP BY Dept;

topics.rl: Indian Railways can report punctuality by zone with GROUP BY Zone and then use HAVING AVG(Delay) > 30 to flag only the zones that need attention.

rv.summary: GROUP BY puts rows with the same value into groups, and aggregates give one result per group. HAVING filters groups using aggregate conditions, while WHERE filters rows before grouping and cannot use aggregates.
focus: Write GROUP BY queries with aggregates
Filter groups with HAVING
Tell WHERE from HAVING
Know the clause order
remember: SELECT Dept, COUNT(*) FROM EMP GROUP BY Dept;
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 filters groups
WHERE filters rows before grouping; no aggregates in WHERE
Order: SELECT ... FROM ... WHERE ... GROUP BY ... HAVING ... ORDER BY
traps: Aggregate conditions go in HAVING, not WHERE
GROUP BY returns one row per group, not every row
Don't think WHERE runs after grouping; it runs before

topics.t: Cartesian product and joins on two tables
topics.h: Student names live in one table and class teachers in another. A join brings them together, and the degree-and-cardinality question about it is almost guaranteed in the board paper.
p: Cartesian product (cross join): every row of the first table is paired with every row of the second. Degree = degree1 + degree2; cardinality = cardinality1 × cardinality2. In SQL: SELECT * FROM STUDENT, CLASS;

Equi-join: keep only the pairs where the common attribute is equal: SELECT * FROM STUDENT, CLASS WHERE STUDENT.ClassID = CLASS.ClassID; or ... FROM STUDENT JOIN CLASS ON STUDENT.ClassID = CLASS.ClassID; The common column appears twice in the output.
Natural join: SELECT * FROM STUDENT NATURAL JOIN CLASS; joins on the common column(s) and shows that column only once.

Table aliases shorten queries and remove ambiguity: SELECT S.Name, C.Teacher FROM STUDENT S, CLASS C WHERE S.ClassID = C.ClassID; A column name found in both tables must be qualified with its table name or alias.
Exam tasks: write queries on given tables, predict query output, create tables with constraints, and differentiate commands (WHERE vs HAVING, DELETE vs DROP, CHAR vs VARCHAR).

ex.q: STUDENT(RollNo, Name, ClassID) has 3 rows: (1, Anu, 11), (2, Bilal, 12), (3, Chitra, 11). CLASS(ClassID, Teacher) has 2 rows: (11, Mr Rao), (12, Ms Iyer). Find the degree and cardinality of STUDENT × CLASS, and the rows of the equi-join.
st: The equi-join keeps the pairs with equal ClassID: Anu–Mr Rao, Bilal–Ms Iyer, Chitra–Mr Rao
ex.a: Cartesian product: degree 5, cardinality 6; equi-join: 3 rows

topics.rl: An online shopping site keeps ORDERS and CUSTOMERS in separate tables and joins them on CustomerID whenever it prints a delivery label with your name and address.

rv.summary: A Cartesian product pairs every row of one table with every row of another (degrees add, cardinalities multiply). An equi-join keeps pairs with equal common values, a natural join shows the common column once, and aliases qualify shared column names.
focus: Find the degree and cardinality of a Cartesian product
Write equi-joins with WHERE or JOIN ... ON
Know how a natural join differs
Qualify ambiguous column names with aliases
remember: Cartesian product: degree = d1 + d2; cardinality = c1 × c2
Equi-join: WHERE A.col = B.col (common column appears twice with SELECT *)
Natural join: common column shown once
Qualify shared columns: S.ClassID
traps: Don't multiply degrees or add cardinalities
Don't leave out the join condition; two tables without it give a Cartesian product
Don't leave a shared column name unqualified; it is ambiguous

topics.ch: Interface of Python with an SQL Database
topics.t: Connecting Python to MySQL
topics.h: Your Python program has the brains and MySQL has the memory. Four lines of code introduce them to each other.
p: Why connect: Python gives the front end (menus, input, calculations, output) while MySQL is the back end that stores data safely and answers queries. Together they make real applications such as a school fee system.
Install the connector once with pip install mysql-connector-python, then import mysql.connector in your program. (pymysql is another connector that works the same way.)

Create a connection object: con = mysql.connector.connect(host='localhost', user='root', passwd='tiger', database='school'). host is the server's address, user and passwd are the MySQL login, and database is the database to use.
con.is_connected() returns True if the connection succeeded, which is useful for checking before you continue.
Create a cursor with cur = con.cursor(). The cursor is the object that sends SQL statements to MySQL and holds the results that come back.

ex.q: Write the statements to connect to the database 'library' on your own computer as user 'root' with password 'admin', confirm the connection and create a cursor.
ex.a: A connection object con and a cursor cur ready to run queries

topics.rl: A school's fee counter app in Python, with MySQL storing every receipt, is exactly the kind of front end–back end pair that CBSE's practical projects ask you to build.

rv.summary: Python acts as the front end and MySQL as the back end of database applications. Install mysql-connector-python, import mysql.connector, connect with host, user, passwd and database, check with is_connected(), and create a cursor with con.cursor().
focus: Explain the front-end and back-end roles
Import the connector and create a connection
Check the connection with is_connected()
Create a cursor and explain its role
remember: pip install mysql-connector-python; import mysql.connector
con = mysql.connector.connect(host='localhost', user='root', passwd='...', database='school')
con.is_connected() returns True if connected
cur = con.cursor(): sends SQL and holds results

cursor() is a method of the connection, not a standalone function
host='localhost' is the server address, not the database name

topics.ch: Interface of Python with an SQL Database
topics.t: Running queries: execute(), commit() and placeholders
topics.h: Your INSERT ran without errors, but the new row isn't in the table. You forgot one word: commit.
p: cur.execute(sql_string) sends any SQL statement to MySQL: CREATE, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE or SELECT.

Changes made by INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE are saved permanently only after con.commit(). Without it, the changes can be lost when the program ends. SELECT and DDL statements such as CREATE TABLE do not need commit().
To put Python values into a query, use %s placeholders and pass a tuple: cur.execute("INSERT INTO student VALUES (%s, %s, %s)", (rno, name, marks)). A single value still needs a tuple: (rno,).
Alternatively build the string with format() or an f-string: "... WHERE rno = {}".format(rno) or f"... WHERE rno = {rno}". Text values then need quotes inside the SQL, e.g. '{}'.
Placeholders are safer than building strings by hand, because the connector quotes the values itself, which protects against SQL injection.

ex.q: Insert a student whose roll number and name are read from the user into STUDENT(rno, name), and save it.

topics.rl: A hospital's patient-registration desk in Python inserts each new patient with placeholders and commits immediately, so the record is safe even if the power goes off a minute later.

rv.summary: cur.execute() sends any SQL statement to MySQL. INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE are saved only after con.commit(). Python values go into queries with %s placeholders and a tuple, or with format() and f-strings.

Know when commit() is needed
Use %s placeholders with a tuple
Build queries with format() and f-strings
remember: cur.execute(sql) runs any SQL statement
con.commit() saves INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE; SELECT needs no commit

Placeholders protect against SQL injection

topics.ch: Interface of Python with an SQL Database
topics.t: Fetching results: fetchone(), fetchall(), fetchmany() and rowcount
topics.h: A SELECT from Python returns nothing visible until you fetch. Choose the right fetch method and you control exactly how many rows you get.
p: After cur.execute('SELECT ...'), rows are fetched through the cursor. fetchone() returns the next row as a tuple, or None if no rows are left.
fetchall() returns all the remaining rows as a list of tuples (an empty list if none remain).
fetchmany(n) returns the next n rows as a list of tuples, or fewer if fewer remain.
cur.rowcount gives the number of rows affected by an INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE. For a SELECT it gives the number of rows fetched so far.
When finished, close the cursor and then the connection: cur.close() and con.close().

ex.q: STUDENT has 5 rows. After cur.execute('SELECT * FROM student'), the program calls fetchone(), then fetchmany(2), then fetchall(). How many rows does each return, and what is cur.rowcount at the end?
st: fetchmany(2) returns the next 2 rows (a list)

topics.rl: An exam portal showing results ten at a time can call fetchmany(10) for each page instead of loading lakhs of rows at once.

Track which rows remain after fetching
Use rowcount for SELECT and DML
Close the cursor and connection correctly

fetchall(): remaining rows as a list of tuples

topics.ch: Interface of Python with an SQL Database
topics.t: Database connectivity applications
topics.h: The CBSE practical file and the 5-mark board question both ask for the same thing: a menu-driven Python program that adds, searches, updates and deletes MySQL records.
p: A menu-driven program shows options in a loop, for example 1 Add, 2 Display, 3 Search, 4 Update, 5 Delete, 6 Exit, and calls a function for each choice.
Insert function: read the values with input(), run INSERT with %s placeholders, then con.commit().
Display or search function: run SELECT (with WHERE for a search), then loop over cur.fetchall() and print each row; if nothing is found, print a message.
Update or delete function: run UPDATE or DELETE with WHERE, then con.commit(); cur.rowcount tells whether any row matched.
Fill-in-the-blank board questions usually leave out one of these: import mysql.connector, connect(...), cursor(), execute(...), commit(), fetchall().

ex.q: Complete the search function: def search(r): cur.execute('SELECT * FROM student WHERE rno = %s', (r,)); row = ______; print(row if row else 'Not found')
st: Only one student can have a given roll number
fetchone() returns that row, or None if there is no match

topics.rl: Small businesses across India, from a kirana store's stock register to a coaching centre's attendance sheet, run on exactly this kind of Python and MySQL menu program.

Build a menu with while True and break

f = open('notes.txt')

f = open('notes.txt')

f = open('notes.txt')

f = open('notes.txt')

line.strip() removes the '\n', leaving 'Hello World' (11), 'Python is fun' (13) and 'Keep coding' (11).

qa.q:

f = open('alpha.txt')
f.read(4)
print(f.tell())

qa.q:
alpha.txt contains ABCDEFGHIJ with no newline. What is the output?
f = open('alpha.txt')
f.seek(6)
print(f.read(2))

qa.q:
alpha.txt contains ABCDEFGHIJ with no newline. What is the output?
f = open('alpha.txt')
f.read()
f.seek(0)

qa.q:
alpha.txt contains ABCDEFGHIJ with no newline. What is the output?
f = open('alpha.txt')
f.seek(0, 2)
print(f.tell())

qa.q:

print(f.read())

qa.q: In f.seek(offset, reference_point), what does reference_point 1 mean?
qa.e: 0 means the beginning, 1 the current position and 2 the end of the file.

qa.q: Kabir wants to add new student names to class.txt every day without losing earlier names. Which statement should he use?

Each line is split into a city and a number; the cities whose number is greater than 10 are Pune (42) and Goa (15).

qa.q: What is pickling?
qa.a: Converting a Python object into a byte stream for storage
qa.e: Pickling serializes an object into bytes so it can be written to a binary file.

qa.q: In which mode should a file be opened before calling pickle.dump() to create a new file of records?
qa.e: pickle writes bytes, so the file must be opened in binary write mode.

qa.q:
What is the output?
import pickle
with open('n.dat', 'wb') as f:
    pickle.dump([10, 20, 30], f)
with open('n.dat', 'rb') as f:
    print(pickle.load(f))
qa.e: load() rebuilds exactly the object that was dumped, a list.

qa.q: Two records were dumped into e.dat. A program calls pickle.load() three times. What happens on the third call?
qa.e: There are no more objects to read, so pickle.load() raises EOFError.
Three objects are dumped. The loop loads them one by one and stops at EOFError, having counted 3.

qa.q: s.dat holds the pickled records {'name': 'Asha', 'marks': 92}, {'name': 'Dev', 'marks': 78} and {'name': 'Zoya', 'marks': 95}, in that order. A program loads each record and prints the name if marks > 90. What is the output?
qa.e: Asha (92) and Zoya (95) have more than 90 marks; Dev (78) does not.

qa.q: Which mode adds new pickled records to the end of an existing binary file without erasing the old ones?
qa.e: 'ab' is binary append mode. 'wb' would erase the existing records.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): A loop that reads all records with pickle.load() is usually written inside try ... except EOFError.
Reason (R): pickle.load() raises EOFError when it tries to read past the last object in the file.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Because reaching the end raises EOFError, catching it is the standard way to stop the loop. R explains A.

qa.q: Why is newline='' passed to open() when writing a CSV file?
qa.a: To prevent extra blank lines between rows
qa.e: The csv writer ends each row with its own line ending; newline='' stops Python adding another translation, which would show as blank rows.

qa.q: What is the difference between writerow() and writerows()?
qa.a: writerow() writes one row; writerows() writes a list of rows
qa.e: writerow() takes one sequence; writerows() takes a sequence of sequences and writes each as a row.

qa.q:

import csv

Each row is a list of strings; int(row[2]) converts the marks. Om (91) and Jai (82) have more than 80.

next(r)

qa.q: Which statement correctly creates a csv writer for the file object f?
qa.e: csv.writer() takes the open file object and returns a writer object.

qa.q: Which of these is TRUE about CSV files?
qa.a: They are text files that a spreadsheet can also open
qa.e: CSV is plain text with comma-separated fields, which spreadsheets and text editors both understand.

qa.q:

qa.q: What does LIFO stand for?
qa.e: In a stack, the last element added is the first to come out.

qa.q: Where are elements added to and removed from in a stack?
qa.e: A stack has a single open end, the top, for both insertion and deletion.

qa.q: Elements 5, 9 and 2 are pushed onto an empty stack in that order. Which element is removed first?
qa.e: 2 was pushed last, so it is on top and comes out first.

qa.q: Which of these applications does NOT naturally use a stack?
qa.a: Serving customers in the order they arrived
qa.e: Serving in order of arrival is first in, first out, which is a queue. The others rely on LIFO.

qa.q: What is a data structure?
qa.a: A way of storing and organising data so it can be used efficiently
qa.e: Data structures such as lists, stacks and queues organise data so that operations on it are efficient.

qa.q: Using a stack to reverse 'RAIL', the letters are pushed in order and then all popped. What is produced?
qa.e: Pushing R, A, I, L puts L on top. Popping gives L, I, A, R.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): A browser's back button can be implemented using a stack.
Reason (R): The most recently visited page is the first one you return to.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Pages are pushed as you visit them; Back pops the most recent one. That LIFO behaviour, described in R, is why a stack fits.

qa.q: Which pair of everyday things are both examples of a stack?
qa.a: A pile of books and a stack of plates
qa.e: In a pile of books or plates you add and remove at the top only. Queues serve people in order of arrival.

qa.q:
What is the output?
S = []
S.append(10)
S.append(20)
S.pop()
S.append(30)
print(S)
qa.e: After the two pushes the stack is [10, 20]. pop() removes the top, 20, and then 30 is pushed.

qa.q: What is the condition called when we try to POP from an empty stack?
qa.e: Underflow means there is nothing to remove. Overflow is pushing onto a full fixed-size stack.

qa.q:
What is the output?
s = [5, 2, 8]
print(s[-1], len(s))

Asha (82) and Ravi (91) score above 75, so they are pushed in that order; popping shows Ravi first.

qa.q:
What happens when this code runs?
st = []
print(st.pop())
